title: Verbs: tense, mood and voice
note: Tense places an action in time; perfect forms (have, had, will have + past participle) show completion, and progressive forms (be + -ing) show action in progress. Mood shows attitude: indicative states, imperative commands, subjunctive marks wishes, conditions contrary to fact and demands ('I insist that he be on time'). In active voice the subject acts; in passive voice it receives the action.

read.title: Choosing voice on purpose
text: In the active voice, the subject of the sentence does the action: "The committee approved the budget." In the passive voice, the subject receives the action, and the doer either moves into a by-phrase or disappears: "The budget was approved (by the committee)." A passive verb always contains a form of be plus a past participle, but not every be verb is passive. "The room was cold" simply describes the room.

Active sentences are usually shorter and more direct, because they tell the reader at once who did what. That is why most style guides advise preferring the active voice. Yet the passive has honest uses. It fits when the doer is unknown ("My bike was stolen"), when the doer does not matter ("The vaccine is stored at low temperatures"), or when you want to keep the reader's attention on the thing acted upon.

The danger is the passive that hides responsibility, as in "Mistakes were made." Who made them? When you revise, find each passive verb and ask whether naming the doer would make the sentence clearer or more honest.

q.q: According to the reading, when does the passive voice fit well?
o: When the doer is unknown or unimportant
Whenever a sentence needs more words
Whenever the verb is in the past tense

q.q: What is the problem with "Mistakes were made"?
o: It hides who made the mistakes
